Muse Ember by @AIatMeta has reshaped the Pareto frontier for Code Arena: WebDev. 

In our last article, we put the AI race under the spotlight and tracked how price-performance trade-offs improved on Code Arena: WebDev from April to October 2026.

But competition never sleeps. Since then, five new models have joined the frontier:
- Claude Fable 5.2 (xHigh) by @AnthropicAI 
- Gemini 4 Carbon (High) by @GoogleDeepMind 
- Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max) by @Kimi_Moonshot 
- GPT-6.1 Terra (Max) by @OpenAI 
- Muse Ember (Max) by @AIatMeta 

Of the five, Muse Ember moved the frontier the most. At about 3 cents an answer, it scores 1608, against 1438 for the previous best at that price. That means it would win about 73% of the time.

Curious how we got here? Full article below.

Alibaba has launched Qwen4 Max, gaining 9 points over Qwen3.8 Max on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and landing 3 points behind Kimi K3.1 Pro at ~11% lower Cost per Task

Qwen4 Max, using xhigh reasoning effort, scores 43 on the Intelligence Index, 9 points ahead of Qwen3.8 Max (xhigh) and 3 points behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (max, 46)

Key takeaways:

➤ Qwen4 Max improves on every evaluation in the Index vs Qwen3.8 Max (xhigh, 34): HLE-Diamond +21 points (24% to 45%), AA-Omniscience +18 points, AutomationBench-AA +17 points, CritPt v2 +13 points, Terminal-Bench-Science +11 points, Terminal-Bench 4.0 +9 points, GDP.pdf +3 points, FrontierCode 2.0 +3 points and AA-Briefcase +82 Elo.

➤ Qwen4 Max costs $3.27 per Intelligence Index task, ~3x less than Qwen3.8 Max ($10.02) and ~11% less than Kimi K3.1 Pro ($3.68): This is driven by 25% lower per-token pricing than Qwen3.8 Max, 70% cheaper cache hits and lower token usage. Tencent Hy4 costs ~3x less per task ($1.03) than Qwen4 Max but scores 8 points lower on the Index.

➤ Qwen4 Max uses 39% fewer output tokens per task than Qwen3.8 Max: ~105k output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs ~171k for Qwen3.8 Max, ~72k for Kimi K3.1 Pro and ~78k for Tencent Hy4. Qwen4 Max uses fewer tokens, while increasing 9 points on the Intelligence Index

➤ Improvements in AA-Briefcase (knowledge work): On AA-Briefcase, our evaluation of agentic work across real business files, Qwen4 Max reaches 1686 Elo vs 1674 for Kimi K3.1 Pro and 1446 for Tencent Hy4.

➤ Qwen4 Max trails Kimi K3.1 Pro on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and Tencent Hy4 on FrontierCode 2.0: Qwen4 Max scores 48% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 vs 67% for Kimi K3.1 Pro and 37% for Tencent Hy4. On FrontierCode 2.0, @cognition’s private evaluation of real-world coding tasks, it scores 26%, level with Kimi K3.1 Pro (26%) and behind Tencent Hy4 (31%).

Key model details:

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodal: Text and image input with text output

➤ Pricing: $1.50/$4.50 per 1M input/output tokens on Alibaba's first-party APIs, with a $0.075 cache hit price. This is lower than Qwen3.8 Max across the board ($2.00/$6.00, with a $0.25 cache hit price)

➤ Availability: @Alibaba_Qwen 's first-party APIs

Announcing Artificial Analysis Time to First Audio, measuring how quickly Text to Speech models start speaking. Among the leading models the wait ranges from 76 ms to nearly a second

Our Text to Speech benchmarks already cover quality, pronunciation and generation speed, but not how long a user waits before hearing anything — the number that decides whether a voice agent feels responsive. We measure every model daily on the same 12 prompts across four input lengths, timing audible speech rather than the first byte, and report a rolling 7-day mean.

Key results:

➤ Fastest at the frontier: @SpeechifyAI's Simba 3.5 starts in 116 ms — the highest Arena Elo of any model that begins speaking in under 200 ms. @InworldAI's Realtime TTS-2 follows at 186 ms.

➤ Turbo variants earn their name: @ElevenLabs' Eleven v4 Turbo starts in 258 ms against 653 ms for Eleven v4, at the same Arena Elo. @FishAudio's Fish Audio Drama 3 matches it at 258 ms and @cartesia's Sonic 3.6 is at 287 ms.

➤ Streaming is the dividing line: The 65 streaming models typically begin speaking within a few hundred milliseconds, a median of 376 ms. The 20 non-streaming models must finish generating before they return anything: a median of 2.0 seconds.

Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf.

A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser, network, filesystem, system fonts. Renders a post to PNG in ~1ms (and 0.4 ms for @jack's "setting up my twttr" 😁).

X is the global town square, and the medium is the message. Being able to preview what things will look like before posting is great for both humans and agents.

Rendering with xeet is is 100x-1000x faster than booting up a browser and taking a screenshot, yet it's just as accurate.

It reproduces Blink & HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64px line breaking, RTL bidi, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK/Math/Emoji fallbacks, "Show more" rules, etc. It's the kind of thing that would be wildly impractical, if not impossible, for a human engineer to pull off.

Except 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝 is structured as an "autorepo." An oracle boots up Chrome, and verifies tens of thousands of text layout rules. A CI canary then watches the evolution of the original, and files signed PRs for agents to act on. It was conceived from the ground up around 'verification engineering', and the result speaks for itself.

Enjoy!

I believe Traces are the essential new primitive of software development and agentic evolution.

Git changed the world by helping us collaborate around the delta unit of code.

Traces are even more powerful than that. They capture the upstream intent, prompts, reasoning, skills and tools use. They are your intelligence.

You should, of course, own and make full use of your intelligence. You start by securely capturing your traces. Then, set up the recursively self-improving systems based on the learnings they contain: friction, latency, outcomes.

Excited to build this future with Tarun and team!

The old way: users are human, you run user interviews, get inspired, mock up user journeys.

The new way: users are agents, you run evals, evals inform the software engineering loop.

tweets.text: even today’s best AI systems, when asked to talk about frontier AI governance and institutions, still have a tendency to mode collapse into 2020-era “consequential decisions” discourse.

this is a very practical example on how to apply agents in a large company setting

babysitting PR is just one use case. i think the good idea here is that everyone can build your own loops and workflows to support specific parts of your work

to start getting your CI under control, it's important to first understand there are a few different types of validations that exist

1. the code follows our rules
2. this change works
3. everything in the main branch works
4. the product is ready to release

traditionally, many codebases run all 4 on every PR as part of their CI pipeline. when every dev merges ~1 PR a day on average, that's doable

but as more and more people can merge 10s or 100s more PRs a day with effective use of agents, their CI starts to struggle. and buying more CI minutes or using faster CI is a losing battle

the solution is to 

- run only #1 and #2 on each PR

and #1 (mostly compile and lint) is typically fast enough that can run as pre-commit hooks as well

on each PR's CI pipeline, try to select only tests that are being edited and relevant to the change, because this is a high frequency bucket and you want to keep this extremely fast

consider assigning a fixed budget such as 5 minutes - whenever the pipeline exceeds that budget, ask an agent to optimize and get it back under the threshold

- run #3 using your merge queue or as a post-push rolling CI pipeline

this is typically your full test suite. running them on every PR at agent speed is simply too much overhead, but you also don't want to fully stop running the full suite, because some problems only occur when multiple changes combine

if you do this post-push, it means your main branch can have problems from time to time. counter-intuitively, that's okay. problems will exist no matter how many tests you run in your CI

when something breaks, fix forward. agents can do this very quickly. and you have a record of which commits pass the full suite - only create releases from those commits

- manage #4 using feature gates and phased rollouts

typically, you should get to a state where anything that could pass #3 is safe to release

in practice though, some problems will only happen with real traffic, so if you are running something at scale, you'd want some gates based on real telemetry

so the pipeline you could create is to release good commits to say 5% of your users, and progressively rollout further only when data looks good

once you have a clean separation of these 4 categories of gates, it'll be easy to know how to optimize and how to make tradeoffs between them

The open-source LLM ecosystem could really benefit from an LLM building-block API.

We have so many LLM components across different models now. Whether you are using PyTorch or C++ and CUDA code directly, there is a major switching cost when you want to run experiments or ablation studies, say swapping GQA with MLA, dense FFNs with MoE, attention layers with Mamba2 or Gated DeltaNet, or standard residual connections with attention residuals.

Currently, it’s very messy even with LLM-assisted coding.

It could maybe be on top of PyTorch or CUDA directly, but it needs to be carefully engineered and maintained (versus quickly vibe-coded on a weekend) and efficient enough that people trust it to use in production (which is really a requirement to move beyond toy examples).

Maybe some food for thought for a big, well-funded lab :)

(There are some efforts that go into that direction, like torchtitan, torchtune, Megatron Core, OLMo-core, but they are not quite that level of abstraction, I'd say. 

And, as always, there’s the chicken-and-egg problem: it needs to be popular to get widely adopted, and it needs to get widely adopted to become popular.)

Someone recently use the phrase "post-AGI partial equilibria" to refer to sci-fi futures like this, and it stuck with me.

Take any sci-fi future with AI and ask: is it a partial or "full" post-AGI equilibrium? Almost all are partial. To sort a few:

When having debates about “Should we pause AI?” I think it’s helpful to first establish a baseline by asking “Do you wish the laws of physics were such that building more advanced AI, from this point forward, would be harder for everyone than it looks like it will be?”

The pause question, for good reason, centers debate on strategy questions like "What would China do?", "Would the pause be 'used well'?", and "Would pausing here be politically tenable?" Asking the baseline question first lets you check agreement on a common premise for the pause debate: We're on a fragile trajectory and the possibility of strong RSI would be an unfortunate fact about the nature of reality, to the extent it puts humanity in a collective action problem.

Getting to ground on the baseline question is sort of a prerequisite for discussing the pause one, since it decides whether you're both fundamentally in a "solutions mindset" about the prospect of strong AI self-improvement and misalignment, or whether the real crux is upstream, like whether these things are plausible enough to be worth worrying about.

There is a developing situation with some U.S. banks. This is not yet confirmed as a cyberattack. But it does seem to be spreading. It started with Chase and Bank of America and now Wells Fargo, Zelle, Capital One, and U.S. Bank are also reporting issues. Logins are down on both web and app, and even some ATMs have stopped working. Transfers are down, and some accounts are showing zero balances.
